wine.name: Columella
wine.grapes: Syrah leads, as it made almost all of the first vintage, with Mourvèdre, Grenache, Carignan, Cinsaut, Tinta Barocca and lately Pinotage in shares that change with the year.
wine.sites: Old, dry farmed bush vines in vineyards across the Paardeberg, the Kasteelberg, Malmesbury and the Piketberg, from the granite of the Paardeberg to the shale and schist of the Kasteelberg; the house blends vineyards rather than grapes.
wine.making: The crop is sorted berry by berry, and the wine ferments with its own yeasts in open concrete tanks for about three weeks, with about three weeks more on the skins. It is basket pressed, goes through malolactic fermentation in barrel, spends about a year in French oak, little of it new, then about a year in large old foudres, and is bottled unfined and unfiltered.
wine.glass: Blackberry, blueberry and black olive over liquorice, tobacco leaf and slate, with a leafy, savoury edge; fresh and dense at once, with fine, layered tannin and a long, savoury finish.
wine.ageing: Tight in its first five years or so; verticals reaching back to its first vintages show it keeping and gaining savoury depth for twenty years.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle an hour or two ahead, an older one gently off its sediment; a large Syrah or Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The name of a Roman writer on farming; the house's white, Palladius, bears the name of another.
The district of the Coastal Region the grapes come from; the seal sets origin, not style.

records.table: Columella is the red of Sadie Family Wines, first made in 2000: Syrah with Mourvèdre, Grenache and other Mediterranean grapes from old dry farmed bush vines across the Swartland. It ferments in open concrete and rests two years in barrels and old foudres, so it pours dense yet fresh.
records.story: The founder worked as a winemaker at Spice Route in the Swartland in the late 1990s, and in 1999 he set up the family's own company, whose first wines were made at Spice Route. Columella was first made with the 2000 vintage, almost all Syrah from old bush vines, and by the house's own account it resolved that year to keep its policies in vineyard and cellar for at least ten years before judging them. Over the years the share of Syrah fell as Mourvèdre and Grenache took a larger part and Carignan, Cinsaut, Tinta Barocca and lately Pinotage joined, for the house came to blend vineyards rather than grapes; Palladius, the white, became its counterpart, and an Old Vine Series later gathered single old parcels from across the Cape. In November 2010 the house was one of the four founders of the Swartland Revolution, a festival first held at Riebeek-Kasteel that ran each year until 2015 and drew the wine trade to a district long known for wheat and bulk wine, and in 2011 a group of the district's growers formed the Swartland Independent Producers. In its own review of twenty vintages, in 2020, the house resolved to use fewer whole bunches. Columella is the wine that first showed what the old vines of the Swartland could give, and a sommelier pours it as the start of that story.

others.name: Palladius
others.note: The white counterpart, a blend of many varieties from old Swartland vines.

others.name: The Old Vine Series
others.note: Single old parcels from across the Cape, among them Skurfberg Chenin Blanc and Pofadder Cinsaut.

traps: Columella is a blend whose share of Syrah has fallen over the years; it is not a varietal Syrah.
Columella is the red and Palladius the white; both carry the names of Roman writers on farming.
Wine of Origin Swartland names the place only; the growers' own style rules come from their association, not from the law.

cards.front: Sadie Family Wines: how has Columella changed since its first vintage of 2000?
cards.back: The first was almost all Syrah; the blend has since widened to Mourvèdre, Grenache, Carignan, Cinsaut, Tinta Barocca and lately Pinotage.

cards.front: Where does Columella ferment, and for how long?
cards.back: With its own yeasts in open concrete tanks, for about three weeks, then about three weeks more on the skins.

questions.q: A guest asks how Sadie Family Wines builds Columella. Which description fits?
opts: Several Swartland vineyards on different soils, blended
One walled vineyard on Paardeberg granite
Grapes bought in from Stellenbosch and Paarl
One parcel of Syrah on schist, bottled alone
questions.exp: The house blends vineyards, not grapes, from the Paardeberg, the Kasteelberg, Malmesbury and the Piketberg; one parcel of Syrah on schist is the way of Porseleinberg and Mullineux, not Columella.

questions.q: In November 2010 Sadie Family Wines and three neighbours founded an event that drew the wine trade to the district each year until 2015. What was it?
opts: The Swartland Revolution
The Old Vine Project
The Cape Wine Auction
The Wine of Origin scheme
questions.exp: The Swartland Revolution was first held at Riebeek-Kasteel in November 2010 and ran until 2015; the Old Vine Project certifies old vineyards and is no festival.

sources.title: The Sadie Family: Columella 2022 technical details
The Sadie Family: The Columella 20 Year Review
Vinous: Fusion over force, The Sadie Family Columella 2001 to 2020
Wikipedia: The Sadie Family
The Wine Society: Back to the Swartland Revolution

report: The making rests on the house's own technical sheets for 2013 to 2024 (sorting, open concrete, three weeks plus three, basket press, malolactic in barrel, a year in barrel and a year in foudre, unfined and unfiltered), with two merchants (Grand Cru Wijnen, Garrafeira Moderna) agreeing on the open concrete; the 20 Year Review gives the policy of 2000 and the scaling back of whole bunches.

The first Columella is 2000 in the house's review, Vinous and Wikipedia; its blend is pure Syrah in Decanter, 90 per cent Syrah in Vinous and 95 per cent in one merchant, so the record says almost all Syrah.
The founder's years at Spice Route rest on Millesima (from 1998) and Wikipedia (early wines made there); Spice Route's founder, who is living, is not named.

The Roman names: Wikipedia says the names allude to the Roman agricultural writers, and the Oxford Companion to Wine holds Columella and Palladius as Roman writers on farming; the record says only that the wine bears a Roman writer's name.

The glass draws on Falstaff's notes of the 2007 and 2008 (blackberry, blueberry, liquorice, olive, tobacco, slate, graphite) and Farr Vintners' note of the 2023 (fresh yet dense, layered); the ageing on the Vinous and Decanter verticals, not on a stated window.

Left out for want of a second source: Palladius first made in 2002, the size of the first vintage, the farm's name (Rotsvast or Rotsvas), Pinotage in the 2024 blend (one search summary of the house's sheet), and the year the Old Vine Series began.

The region record's growers' charter of 2010: the sources read give 2011 for the forming of the Swartland Independent Producers (Farmers Weekly and two more), so the story says 2011 and the trap gives no year.

The library's Sadie record carries the country field Australia, New Zealand, South Africa and South America, which looks like a section heading rather than a country; the Decanter vertical was read but not cited, since its address carries the founder's name. No swap proposed.

records.place: Roundstone farm on the Kasteelberg, near Riebeek-Kasteel, Swartland

wine.name: Mullineux Schist Syrah
wine.grapes: Syrah alone, from a single parcel of the home farm.
wine.sites: One parcel on the stony shale and schist of Roundstone, the house's own farm on the slopes of the Kasteelberg near Riebeek-Kasteel, where the rocky soil keeps the vines small.
wine.making: The whole bunches are crushed by foot into open 500 litre barrels and ferment with their own yeasts for about ten days, with plunging by hand only, then stay about four weeks on the skins. The wine ages about a year in 500 litre French oak barrels, from a quarter to a half of them new, then nine or ten months in a 2,000 litre foudre, and is bottled unfined and unfiltered.
wine.glass: Blackberry and damson plum over cracked black pepper, charcoal, graphite and sage, with a flinty, ashen edge; dense and structured, with fine but plentiful tannin and a long, firm finish.
wine.ageing: Firm and dense when young, darker and more structured than the house's Granite; by the house's own account it drinks well over fifteen to twenty five years.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or two; a large Syrah or Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The soil of the parcel, the shale and schist of the Kasteelberg, which names the wine.
The house's own farm on the Kasteelberg, printed on the label beside the word Schist.
The district the grapes come from; the seal sets origin, not style.

records.table: Mullineux Schist Syrah is one of the house's single soil Syrahs: whole bunches from one parcel of shale and schist on its home farm on the Kasteelberg, aged in barrels and then a large foudre. It is darker and firmer than the Granite, so decant it.
records.story: The house was founded in 2007 by a winemaking couple who settled at Riebeek-Kasteel in the Swartland. Their first Syrah, of the 2008 vintage, was made at Reyneke in Stellenbosch, where they were then making wine. In November 2010 they were among the four founders of the Swartland Revolution, a festival first held at Riebeek-Kasteel that ran each year until 2015 and brought buyers and writers to a district long known for bulk wine. The same 2010 vintage began their single soil range: Syrah from schist and Syrah from granite, bottled apart so that the soils could be read side by side. The Schist parcel lies on Roundstone, the house's own farm on the slopes of the Kasteelberg. In 2013 the couple took a partner, and the business became Mullineux and Leeu Family Wines, with a second cellar, Leeu Passant, in Franschhoek. A Syrah from iron rich soil later joined the range, beside Chenin Blanc from quartz, and the Syrahs make the case that Syrah, not Pinotage, is the Swartland's red. For a sommelier the Schist is the district's geology in a glass: one grape, one way of making, and a soil that names the bottle.

others.name: Mullineux Granite Syrah
others.note: The perfumed, higher toned counterpart from granite, the direct comparison wine.

others.name: Mullineux Quartz Chenin Blanc
others.note: Old vine Chenin Blanc from one soil, taut and stony.

others.name: Mullineux Straw Wine
others.note: Sweet Chenin Blanc from grapes dried before pressing, unfortified.

traps: Schist and Granite are two Syrahs of one house bottled by soil; Granite is the perfumed, higher toned wine, Schist the darker and firmer.
Mullineux Straw Wine is sweet from grapes dried before pressing; it is not fortified.
Swartland Syrah of this kind is perfumed and medium to full bodied, not a warm climate blockbuster.

cards.front: Mullineux Schist Syrah: where does its parcel lie?
cards.back: On the stony shale and schist of Roundstone, the house's own farm on the Kasteelberg near Riebeek-Kasteel.

cards.front: How does Mullineux begin the fermentation of its Schist Syrah?
cards.back: Whole bunches are crushed by foot into open 500 litre barrels and ferment with their own yeasts.

questions.q: A guest compares Mullineux Schist Syrah with the house's Granite Syrah. What sets the two apart?
opts: The soil each parcel grows on
The grape, Syrah against Grenache
Fortification of one of the two
A share of white grapes in one
questions.exp: The house bottles the two apart by soil so that the soil can be read; both are Syrah alone, and neither is fortified.

questions.q: The Mullineux house was founded in 2007. With which vintage did its single soil Syrahs, Schist and Granite, begin?
questions.exp: The single soil range began with the 2010 vintage; 2008 was the house's first Syrah, made at Reyneke, and 2013 the year of the Leeu partnership.

sources.title: Liberty Wines: Mullineux Single Terroir Schist Swartland Syrah
Mullineux and Leeu: 2022 Schist Roundstone Syrah fact sheet
Skurnik Wines: Mullineux Syrah Schist Roundstone
Winemag: Mullineux Schist Syrah vertical
The Wine Society: Back to the Swartland Revolution

report: The house's own domain gave no search results, so the making rests on its technical sheets as the distributor Meridian publishes them (2017, 2018, 2020, 2023) and on Skurnik's notes: foot crushed whole bunches in open 500 litre barrels, natural yeasts, a year in 500 litre barrels half new, nine or ten months in a 2,000 litre foudre, unfined and unfiltered.

The first Mullineux Syrah of 2008 made at Reyneke and the 2010 start of the single soil range both rest on winemag.co.za (its Schist vertical and its review of the range), with a second account, on a writer's own site not cited, that the couple rented space at Reyneke for their first vintages; the checker may want a second publication for 2010.

Left out for want of a second source: the year Roundstone was bought (winemag says only that the couple had worked the vineyard since 2005), the planting year of the parcel (2000 in winemag, and vine ages that do not agree in the sheets), the separation of the two cellars from the 2018 vintage, and the couple leaving a Tulbagh cellar in 2007.

The glass draws on critics' notes quoted by Skurnik (flint, cracked black pepper, charcoal, sage, damson, blackberry, ash, graphite, fine but abundant tannin) and Liberty Wines (dark fruit, structured, dense); the ageing on the house's 2018 sheet (fifteen to twenty five years).
The say field is empty: no source read gave how the family name is said, and a guess would teach a wrong sound.
The Leeu partner of 2013, who is living, is not named; the library's holdings line names him and the couple, which the record does not repeat. No swap proposed.

records.place: Kalmoesfontein farm on the Paardeberg, Swartland

wine.name: AA Badenhorst Family White Blend
wine.grapes: Old bush vine Chenin Blanc leads, with smaller shares of Roussanne, Grenache Blanc, Viognier, Verdelho, Semillon and Palomino, the mix changing with the year.
wine.sites: Small parcels across Kalmoesfontein on the Paardeberg, mostly old, unirrigated bush vines planted from the 1950s onwards on the hill's granite.
wine.making: The parcels are picked on the same day and pressed together as whole bunches, and the juice ferments as one wine in large old foudres. The wine then rests in them on its lees for about a year before bottling.
wine.glass: Citrus blossom, white peach and pear over tea leaf, fynbos and rose petal; broad, textured and ripe, with gentle grip and a long, savoury finish that turns towards dried honey and undergrowth with age.
wine.ageing: Open and generous on release; it keeps for some years more, gaining notes of dried honey and undergrowth as it goes.
wine.serve: 10 to 13 degrees Celsius, not too cold; no need to decant; a wide white wine glass.

label.means: The home farm on the Paardeberg, whose name the same white blend has carried in place of Family White.
The district the grapes come from; the seal sets origin, not style.

records.table: AA Badenhorst Family White Blend, sold lately under its farm's name, Kalmoesfontein, is old bush vine Chenin Blanc pressed and fermented together with Roussanne, Grenache Blanc and other white grapes of the Paardeberg, in large old foudres. It is broad, textured and savoury.
records.story: The house was founded by two cousins of a Constantia family whose grandfather managed the farm at Groot Constantia for decades. One of them made wine at Rustenberg in Stellenbosch before, in 2008, the two bought Kalmoesfontein, an old farm on the Paardeberg in the Swartland. The farm's cellar had last made wine in the 1930s and stood neglected, and the cousins began, by the house's account, by restoring it and planting new vines beside the old bush vines already there, many of them planted in the 1950s and 1960s. The farm's buildings run back further: the Koringhuis, the old grain store, dates by the house's account to the late eighteenth century. In November 2010 the house was one of the four founders of the Swartland Revolution, the festival first held at Riebeek-Kasteel that ran each year until 2015 and drew the wine trade to the district. Its white blend was long sold as the Family White, and it later took the farm's name, Kalmoesfontein, while some merchants kept the old one. Its grapes, from small parcels across the farm, are picked on one day and fermented together, so the wine is a field blend made as one. For a sommelier it is the Swartland white blend in its plainest form: many grapes, one farm, one ferment.

others.name: Kalmoesfontein Red Blend
others.note: The red counterpart, also a field blend of the farm, its grapes picked on the same day.

others.name: Secateurs Chenin Blanc
others.note: The house's younger Chenin Blanc, drawn from parcels in and around the Paardeberg.

traps: The Family White Blend and the Kalmoesfontein White Blend are one wine under its old and new names, not two wines.
Its grapes are co-fermented as one wine, not fermented apart and blended afterwards.
Kalmoesfontein is the Badenhorst farm on the Paardeberg; Columella and Palladius are Sadie wines from the same hill.

cards.front: AA Badenhorst Family White Blend: which grape leads it?
cards.back: Old bush vine Chenin Blanc, with Roussanne, Grenache Blanc, Viognier and other white grapes in smaller shares.

cards.front: On which hill of the Swartland did the Badenhorst cousins buy Kalmoesfontein in 2008?

questions.q: A guest asks how the AA Badenhorst Family White Blend is put together. Which answer fits?
opts: Grapes pressed together and co-fermented in old foudres
Each grape fermented apart in steel, then blended
Chenin Blanc alone from one young vineyard
Grapes dried on straw before a sweet ferment
questions.exp: The farm's parcels are picked on one day, pressed together and fermented as one wine in large old foudres; it is many white grapes, not Chenin Blanc alone.

questions.q: When the Badenhorst cousins bought Kalmoesfontein in 2008, when had its old cellar last made wine?
opts: In the 1930s
In the 1870s
In the 1990s
In the 1700s
questions.exp: The cellar had stood unused since the 1930s, and the cousins restored it first; the Koringhuis, not the cellar, dates to the late eighteenth century.

AA Badenhorst Family Wines: Kalmoesfontein Wine Collection
Liberty Wines: AA Badenhorst Kalmoesfontein White Blend
The Wine Society: A. A. Badenhorst Kalmoesfontein White Blend 2018
Broadbent Selections: A. A. Badenhorst Family

report: The wine is the same one under two names: the Wine Society's listings of 2011, 2014 and 2018 call the Kalmoesfontein White previously known as the Family White, and Bordeaux Index says it is now named after the home farm; the house's own pages and Liberty Wines use Kalmoesfontein White Blend, while wine.com still lists Badenhorst Family White Blend to the 2023 vintage.

Proposed for the read-together agent, in the way of the Pfalz ruling: keep the key and the house and change the plan's wine to Kalmoesfontein White Blend, the name the house itself now gives it; the record keeps the plan's words until then, as the lint requires, and teaches the new name on the label and in the traps.
founded is 2008 by the house's own About page (the cousins bought the farm in 2008); one merchant says 2007, so the checker may wish to see it again.

The making rests on the house's collection page (picked from small parcels, pressed together whole bunch, co-fermented in old casks) and Liberty Wines (natural fermentation, about twenty months in old French oak foudres and 500 litre barrels); the record says a year or more in old foudres since wine.com gave twelve months in foudre for the 2017 and Broadbent says lightly wooded in old foudres; natural fermentation and the 500 litre barrels are in Liberty alone and left out.

The grapes are those named in at least two of Liberty Wines, wine.com (the 2019 at about half Chenin Blanc) and a merchant's listing; Clairette Blanche, Colombar, Marsanne, Muscat of Alexandria and Sauvignon Blanc appear in one each and are left out.

The granite of the Paardeberg is the region record's; the farm's own soil was not in any source read. The grandfather's 46 years at Groot Constantia, nine years at Rustenberg and the first vintage of the white were each in one source only and are left out or said without the figure.
The cousins are living and not named; one of them is already in people.json, and the other cousin's name should be added. No swap of the house proposed.

records.place: A schist ridge near Riebeek-Kasteel, Swartland

wine.name: Porseleinberg Syrah
wine.grapes: Syrah alone, from the farm's own vineyards.
wine.sites: Steep, rocky slopes of decomposed mica schist on hard bedrock, the schist bluer on the upper slopes and redder, richer in iron, lower down.
wine.making: The grapes are fermented largely or wholly as whole bunches, and since 2018 the cap of skins has been kept mostly submerged in the juice rather than pumped over. The wine then matures for about a year, the great part in large foudres and a small share in concrete eggs, before bottling.
wine.glass: Red cherry, rose petal and cracked pepper over rosemary, thyme and overturned earth, with an iron, smoky note; wild and savoury, firm yet fine, with a long, peppery finish.
wine.ageing: Closed for its first five or six years; merchants then give it ten to fifteen years more in bottle, and it gains complexity as it goes.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for two hours or more; a large Syrah or Bordeaux glass.

label.means: Porcelain mountain in Afrikaans: the farm's name, and the wine's.
The district the grapes come from; the seal sets origin, not style.

records.table: Porseleinberg Syrah is the single wine of a schist ridge near Riebeek-Kasteel that Boekenhoutskloof bought in 2009: whole bunches, matured mostly in large foudres with a little in concrete eggs. Peppery, wild and savoury, it wants five years in bottle.
records.story: Porseleinberg, porcelain mountain in Afrikaans, is a farm on a rugged schist ridge near Riebeek-Kasteel in the Swartland. In 2009 Boekenhoutskloof, the Franschhoek house, bought it, by its own account to secure a reliable source of quality grapes, Syrah above all. The first wine came with the 2010 vintage, and the farm has made one wine ever since: a Syrah under the farm's own name. That November Porseleinberg was among the four founders of the Swartland Revolution, the festival first held at Riebeek-Kasteel that ran each year until 2015 and drew buyers and writers to a district long known for bulk wine. The vineyard is decomposed mica schist on hard, rocky bedrock, and the wine is made to show it: whole bunches, large foudres and concrete rather than small new barrels. The label is printed by hand on a vintage Heidelberg letterpress in the farm's own cellar. The Franschhoek house's own Syrah draws largely on the same vineyard, with fruit from Goldmine, a second Swartland farm, but Porseleinberg bottles the ridge alone. For a sommelier it is the Swartland's schist told through one grape on one farm.

others.name: Boekenhoutskloof Syrah
others.note: Not a Porseleinberg wine but the Franschhoek house's own Syrah, drawn largely from the Porseleinberg vineyard with fruit from its Goldmine site.

traps: Porseleinberg is a single Syrah under the farm's own name; Boekenhoutskloof Syrah, though largely from the same vineyard, is a different wine.
Porseleinberg grows on schist; the granite of the Swartland is the Paardeberg's.
Whole bunches and large foudres make it peppery and savoury, not a ripe, oaky warm climate Shiraz.

cards.front: Porseleinberg Syrah: on what soil does it grow?
cards.back: Decomposed mica schist on hard, rocky bedrock, on a ridge near Riebeek-Kasteel.

cards.front: How is the Porseleinberg label printed?
cards.back: By hand, on a vintage Heidelberg letterpress in the farm's own cellar.

questions.q: A guest asks why Porseleinberg Syrah tastes of pepper and herbs rather than sweet oak. Which reason fits?
opts: Whole bunches and large foudres, not small new barrels
Long ageing in small new American oak
A share of Viognier fermented with the Syrah
Grapes from warm, deep alluvial soils
questions.exp: It is fermented largely as whole bunches and matured mostly in large foudres, with a little in concrete eggs, so oak stays in the background; it is Syrah alone, with no Viognier.

questions.q: Which house bought the Porseleinberg farm in 2009, by its own account to secure a supply of Syrah?
opts: Boekenhoutskloof of Franschhoek
Sadie Family Wines of the Paardeberg
Mullineux of Riebeek-Kasteel
Allesverloren of Riebeek West
questions.exp: Boekenhoutskloof bought the farm in 2009, and the wine has been made since the 2010 vintage; Sadie and Mullineux were its fellow founders of the Swartland Revolution, not its owners.

sources.title: Boekenhoutskloof: Milestones
Boekenhoutskloof: Syrah 2021 fact sheet
Berry Bros and Rudd: 2022 Porseleinberg, Swartland
Farr Vintners: Porseleinberg Syrah 2020
Visi: Porseleinberg letterpress labels

report: founded is empty: Boekenhoutskloof's own Milestones page dates the purchase to 2009 and the first vintage is 2010 (Roberson Wine, Caviste, the Vinous vertical of 2010 to 2020), but the farm stood before it was bought, so neither year is a founding.
The soil rests on Boekenhoutskloof's fact sheets (decomposed mica schist on hard, rocky bedrock) and the Vinous vertical (blue schist above, redder and more ferrous below).

The making rests on Berry Bros and Rudd and Farr Vintners across the 2019, 2020, 2022 and 2024 vintages (whole bunches, submerged cap, about twelve months, mostly in large foudres with five to fifteen per cent in concrete eggs or vats); Farr's archive dates the submerged cap to 2018 and an early split of concrete and foudre, each in that one source, so the record gives neither year.

The ageing rests on Berry Bros and Rudd (five or six years in bottle first; windows to 2035 and 2042) and the Wine Society (2028 to 2039 for the 2024); the glass on the notes quoted by the two merchants (pepper, rosemary, thyme, iron, red cherry, rose petal, overturned earth, smoke).

The letterpress label is in Visi, Vinfolio's editorial and The Dieline; the press's decade (the 1940s) is in one source and is left out. Organic farming, often said of the farm, was in no source read and is left out.
Living names for people.json: the Boekenhoutskloof founder who bought the farm, the farm's first farmer and winemaker (2009 to 2024 by one account) and his successor; none is named in the record.
The region record's producers line calls Porseleinberg the Swartland's single site benchmark, a judgement word the flagship rules refuse; the record does not repeat it. No swap proposed.

wine.name: Allesverloren Fine Old Vintage
wine.grapes: Led by Tinta Barocca, Touriga Nacional and Souzão; the estate speaks of seven grapes in the wine, with Tinta Roriz and Tinta Francisca among the others.
wine.sites: The estate's own trellised vineyards at Riebeek West in the Swartland, where the family grew Portuguese grapes for its fortified wine.
wine.making: The grapes are picked by hand and fermented on their skins, and the wine is fortified with grape spirit before all its sugar has fermented, the method of port. It then spends about twenty months in French oak barrels before bottling, while a Reserve is held six years in oak.
wine.glass: Deep ruby, with fresh grape and warm cinnamon on the nose; sweet, soft and velvety in the mouth, smooth rather than fiery, with a long finish of rich fruitcake.
wine.ageing: Made to drink on release, soft and smooth, as the estate presents it; like other Cape Vintages it can also be kept, softening further in bottle over the years.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant an older bottle off any sediment; a port glass, with aged cheese.

label.means: The name the estate gives this wine from the 2020 vintage: the Cape term for a port style wine of one year.
The name the same wine carried on its label before the estate renamed it Cape Vintage.
All is lost: the farm's name since 1704, after a fire, as the story goes.

records.table: Allesverloren Fine Old Vintage, labelled Cape Vintage from the 2020 vintage, is the port style red of a Riebeek West farm the Malan family took over in 1872: Tinta Barocca, Touriga Nacional and Souzão, fortified and aged about twenty months in French oak. It is sweet, velvety and rich.
records.story: The estate's own history places its beginning between 1696 and 1704, when, as the house tells it, the governor of the Cape left the land to a widow named Cloete. The story goes that in 1704 the family came home from a journey to Stellenbosch to find the house burnt and the farm in ruins, and the farm took its name, Allesverloren, all is lost. In 1872 the Malan family took over the farm, and on 22 May 1874 Daniel François Malan (1874 to 1959) was born there; he became prime minister of South Africa from 1948 to 1954, and his government brought in apartheid. By the family's own account a Malan of the farm first made the fortified wine that grew into its flagship, and the family were pioneers in bringing Portuguese grapes to South Africa. The wine was long sold as Allesverloren Port. Under a wine agreement signed with the European Union in 2002, South Africa gave up the Portuguese name; the estate's wine became Fine Old Vintage, and from the 2020 vintage it has been called Cape Vintage. Beside it the estate kept Tinta Barocca and Shiraz as dry table wines. To a sommelier it is the Swartland's older fortified tradition, made from the grapes of port, beside the district's newer dry reds.

others.name: Allesverloren Fine Old Vintage Reserve
others.note: A reserve of the fortified wine, held six years in older French oak before bottling.

others.name: Allesverloren Tinta Barocca
others.note: A dry red of the Portuguese grape that also leads the fortified wine.

others.name: Allesverloren Shiraz
others.note: The estate's dry Shiraz from its Riebeek West vineyards.

traps: Fine Old Vintage and Cape Vintage are one wine under its old and new names, not two wines.
Allesverloren's fortified wine is from the Swartland, not from Calitzdorp, the Klein Karoo district known for Cape port style wine.
Allesverloren means all is lost; the name comes from a fire of 1704, as the story goes, not from the wine.

cards.front: Allesverloren Fine Old Vintage: which three grapes lead it?
cards.back: Tinta Barocca, Touriga Nacional and Souzão, Portuguese grapes of port.

cards.front: What does the name Allesverloren mean, and where does it come from?
cards.back: All is lost: as the story goes, the family came home from a journey in 1704 to find the farm burnt.

questions.q: A guest asks why Allesverloren's fortified red no longer says port on its label. What is the reason?
opts: A wine agreement with the European Union
A change of style to a dry table wine
A move of its vineyards to the Klein Karoo
A switch to a blend of several vintages
questions.exp: Under its wine agreement with the European Union, signed in 2002, South Africa gave up the name port; the estate's wine became Fine Old Vintage and, from 2020, Cape Vintage, fortified and of one year as before.

questions.q: Allesverloren took its name, all is lost, after an event of 1704. What was it, as the story goes?
opts: The farm burnt while the family was away
A flood washed away the first vineyards
The governor took the land back
A shipwreck lost the first harvest
questions.exp: As the estate tells it, the family came home from a journey to find the house destroyed and the farm in ruins; the governor's part was to leave the land to the widow Cloete.

report: founded is empty: the estate's own history says its records are unclear and places its beginning between 1696 and 1704, the year the name was given; the plan's why (a farm of 1704) and the region line (granted in 1704) say more than the house does.

The flagship's name has changed: the estate's own page for the wine, at the address allesverloren-fine-old-vintage, now calls it Allesverloren Cape Vintage, and Aspire Lifestyle and one more summary date the change to the 2020 vintage. Proposed for the read-together agent, in the way of the Pfalz ruling: keep the key and change the plan's wine to Allesverloren Cape Vintage; the record keeps the plan's words until then, as the lint requires.

The grapes rest on the estate's page (seven grapes; Tinta Barocca, Touriga Nacional and Souzão in thirds for the 2022), Systembolaget (Tinta Barocca, Souzão, Pontac, Malvasia, Tinta Roriz, Tinta Francisca, Touriga Nacional for the 2021) and a merchant's list with Tinta Francisca; Malvasia Rey and Tinta Roriz are in fewer sources and left out.

The making's twenty months in French oak is the estate's page for the 2022; the six years in oak is its page for the Fine Old Vintage Reserve 2014. The serve follows the estate's slightly chilled, at the cool edge of the Codex's 16 to 18 for Vintage Port.

Daniel François Malan's birth on the farm on 22 May 1874, his death in 1959 and his years as prime minister are in Wikipedia, South African History Online, Britannica and a genealogy page; the Malan who first made the fortified wine is not identified in the house's account, so he is not named.

Left out for want of a second source: the planting of Portuguese grapes in 1939, a first wine under the estate's name in 1972, shale soils and dry farming, and the glass beyond the estate's own note and one merchant's (velvety, fruitcake finish); the ageing has no window for this wine in any source read.

The Codex's data-intro says Cape Vintage does its ageing in bottle rather than in wood; this one spends about twenty months in oak first, which fits a vintage style but is worth a line if the integrator reads them together. No swap of the house proposed.
